Where it began

Hashim Amla was born in Durban on 31 March 1983 and went to Durban High School, which had already produced Barry Richards and Lance Klusener. Cricket ran in the family: his elder brother Ahmed played the game professionally, starting two years ahead of him, and the pair later lined up together for the KwaZulu-Natal Dolphins. Hylton Ackerman, a former Western Province captain, saw his talent early and helped to polish it.

He led South Africa at the 2002 Under-19 World Cup in New Zealand and took them to the final. At 21 he was captain of KwaZulu-Natal, and he opened the 2004–2005 season with four hundreds in his first eight innings.

The player

His Test debut came at Eden Gardens in Kolkata in November 2004. The start was slow and his technique drew criticism, so he went back to the Dolphins and worked on it. The reward came at Newlands in 2006, when his 149 against New Zealand helped save a Test. From then on he was a fixture at number three.

In 2010 he made 253 not out against India, and in 2012 at The Oval he batted all the way to 311 not out, South Africa's first Test triple hundred, in an innings win over England. A hundred at Lord's in the same series helped take his side to the top of the Test rankings. In January 2017 he marked his 100th Test with a century, only the second South African after Graeme Smith to do so. In all he played 124 Tests, scoring 9,282 runs at 46.64 with 28 hundreds and 41 fifties, and held 108 catches.

What made him special

Consistency, above all: averaging 46.64 from 2004 to 2019 does not happen by accident. The ICC picked him in its World Test XI for 2010 and 2011, and again for 2012 and 2013, and from 2014 he captained South Africa in 14 Tests, winning his first series as captain in Sri Lanka. With Jacques Kallis he formed one of his country's great Test partnerships.

His bowling was another matter. He did send down a few overs in Tests, but the wicket column stayed blank.

Away from the middle

He enjoyed four spells in English county cricket, with Essex, Nottinghamshire, Surrey and Derbyshire. At Essex in 2009 he made 181 on debut, at the time the highest by an Essex debutant, and the supporters took to calling him W. G., after W. G. Grace. Later came Twenty20 cricket around the world and, from 2023, a role as batting coach of the Lions in Johannesburg.

Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year, and his country honoured him with the Order of Ikhamanga in Silver. He was also named South African Sport Star of the Year.

And finally

One record came with a wry smile. In 2016, out lbw to Nuwan Pradeep at St George's Park, he became the 10,000th lbw victim in the history of Test cricket. Nobody aims for that milestone, but somebody had to reach it.
